newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Consumers likely to absorb higher costs for airlines.
newsitem.headline: Consumers likely to absorb higher costs for airlines.

text.p: As international airlines are poised to report record profits this year, soaring fuel costs and mounting regulatory charges are likely to be absorbed by passengers as the companies pass on the higher costs.
"There is a limit to how much can be absorbed by the airlines," Pierre Jeanniot, director-general of the International Air Transport Association, told the group's annual meeting Monday.
He said profits for its more than 250 member carriers this year should reach $5.5 billion, below the $6 billion he predicted in April.
"On revenues of $128.8 billion that represents only 4 percent. It may not seem very high, but in dollar terms it is still an all-time record," Jeanniot said in a report on the state of the industry.
American Airlines Chairman Robert Crandall told the group that his company's fuel costs so far this year have risen by between $300 million and $400 million due to rising jet fuel prices.
"Fuel is a big worry. For every one cent rise in fuel prices, our bill rises by $30 million a year," he said.
Crandall said American "had done some modest hedging" and that "higher costs were always a cause for concern."

He declined to comment when asked whether the airline intended to raise passenger fares following its announcement Friday that it was introducing a 10 cents a kilogram (2.2 pounds) cargo fuel surcharge on most of its international routes, excluding trans-Pacific flights. The surcharge is effective Nov. 15.
The move followed similar hikes in cargo prices by major European airlines after Deustche Lufthansa AG led the way on Oct. 25.
Lufthansa Chairman Juergen Weber said his company would also hike passenger prices this month, though he said the amount would vary by market.
IATA has called an emergency meeting for Nov. 13 in Geneva to discuss the price increases.

As airlines climb out of the recession of the early 1990s, when they suffered losses of $15.2 billion, they face rising fuel prices, which account for between 10 percent to 20 percent of their costs. In addition, they pay for airport use and air traffic control services, which account for about 10 percent of operating costs, Jeanniot and other officials said.
Jeanniot, a former chief of Air Canada, noted a growing consensus among airlines that part of the higher costs must be borne by travelers.
"All our airlines have one thing in common. We are not making enough money," said Otto Loepfe, president of IATA and Swissair.
